en: In the "Chapter on the Mirror-Lamps of the Avataṃsaka," the Śramaṇa Ciyun of Qingze compiled this work with his disciple Rulang.
For those who have not yet fully realized the principle of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena within the Dharma-realm, he established skillful means. Regarding...
In a single dark room, five Buddha images are enshrined, each illuminated by a lamp placed before it.

Ten circular mirrors are taken and arranged in the ten directions so that they face one another, their reflections intersecting with one another. Through this, the student awakens to and enters the principle of the ocean of lands (*kṣetra-samudra*), wherein realms interpenetrate in layers upon layers without end.
Now, based on this very analogy, I shall expound upon the hundred gates of the Dharma of the Honored One (Bodhidharma).
First, regarding the times of illumination: before the first Buddha in the east, at dawn, a lamp is lit to dispel the darkness; this is the initial illumination of the *Avataṃsaka* assembly.
Before the second Buddha to the east, at midday, a lamp is lit to dispel the darkness; this is the first turning of the *Āgama* assembly.

Before the third Buddha in the center, at the hour of the afternoon meal, a lamp is lit to dispel the darkness; this is the middle turning of the *Saṃdhinirmocana* assembly. Before the fourth Buddha near the west... [text continues].
After noon, one lights lamps to dispel the darkness; this is later followed by the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, both of which are termed "times of turning and illuminating.
(2) Before the fifth Buddha of the Western Quarter, as evening falls, one lights lamps to dispel the darkness; this returns to the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* assembly. (3)
(4) Within a single kṣaṇa, five lamps suddenly arise, instantly shattering the thousand-year-old darkness of a room and manifesting the images of Buddhas within mirrors throughout the ten directions;
this is called "merely based on a single thought-moment. (5) Not only is it thus for a kṣaṇa, but it is likewise so throughout an entire day;
this is called "completely encompassing a single transformation. (6) Since it is so in the present, it is likewise so in the past and future; this is called "pervasive."
(6) The three periods [of the day]. When the shadow appears at this noon, it is identical to that of yesterday’s noon and tomorrow’s noon; this is called "subsuming similar kalpas.
(7) When the shadow appears last evening and this morning, it is identical to that of tomorrow morning and noon; this is called "gathering dissimilar kalpas.
(8) Since the three illuminations each day do not differ from a single thought-moment, this present thought-moment subsumes many days; this is called "using the thought-moment."
(9) The kalpa is subsumed by thought-moments (*kṣaṇa*). Within a day there are thought-moments; since the thought-moment already subsumes the day, the day exists within the thought-moment.

Furthermore, the day contains many thought-moments; as the thought-moments are inexhaustible, the days are likewise infinite. This is called the "kalpa of the repeated inclusion of thought-moments. (10) Just as it is with the days and thought-moments in a single room, so it is with the days and thought-moments in many rooms.
This is called the "kalpa of the realms of different categories" (*nānā-jātīya-dhātu-kalpa*). (11) This single day’s thought-moment [is related to] that...
(12) Many days of mindfulness mutually encompass and mutually enter one another; this is called "the mutual encompassing and entering of this and that.

Originally there was no time or mindfulness, but by relying on the mirror and the lamp, time and mindfulness are established. Since the mirror and the lamp are eternally pervasive, time and mindfulness are eternally pervasive; this is called "gathering the derivative within the fundamental."
(13) The above metaphors illustrate the three periods in both their general and specific aspects.
Next, the ritual procedure is described: a single mirror-lamp in the east serves as the root, while the mirror-lamps in the other directions serve as the branches.

When the reflection of the root and the reflections of the branches are equal from beginning to end, it is called the "Root-and-Branch Gate" (Benmo Men). (14) When the eastern mirror-lamp is divided and its light reaches the western lamp, it is called the "Arising-of-the-Branched-Gate" (Qimomen).

(15) Gathering the shadows and light from the west back to the eastern location is called the Gate of Returning to the Source. (16) The original lamp and the derivative lamps mutually accomplish one another without obstruction;
this is called the Gate of Non-obstruction. (17) Sometimes one sees a single lamp, and sometimes one sees many lamps, each according to the capacity of the individual;
this is called the Gate of Indeterminacy. (18) Sometimes one sees this lamp and does not see that lamp; sometimes both see that lamp, or sometimes they do not see one another.

The Gate of Revealing the Exoteric and Esoteric (19). The mirror, lamp, light, and shadow—manifesting the fundamental and the derivative, the one and the many—all appear simultaneously and instantaneously;

this is called the Gate of Sudden Manifestation (20). The one and many shadows and lights are fundamentally empty and quiescent; this is called the Gate of Stillness and Silence (21). Throughout the limits of the past and future, the mirror and lamp are likewise so;
this is called the Gate of Universal Pervasion (22). Interacting from time to time and pervading everywhere; this is called the Gate of Non-... [the text here is incomplete].
The Section on the Gate of Exhaustion (23).
Third, the classification by teaching: the mirror, lamp, and Buddha-image arise from causes and conditions; this is the Small Teaching (24). It establishes the characteristics of dharmas.

(25) To establish the characteristics by means of consciousness-only is called "establishing characteristics" (*xiāng*). That the causal conditions of dharmic characteristics are ultimately and thoroughly empty is called "destroying characteristics" (*pò xiāng*);

both belong to the Initial Teaching (*shǐ jiào*). (26) Although this is ultimately and thoroughly empty, it does not obstruct the dependent origination (*yuánqǐ*) of the storehouse-consciousness (*zàngxīn*);

this is the Final Teaching (*zhōng jiào*). (27) Although illusory existence remains manifest, it does not obstruct the quiescent extinction (*jìmíè*) of true nature; this is the Sudden Teaching (*dùn jiào*). The Lamp and Light.
Like mirror-images, they are simultaneously pervasive and encompass one another in infinite layers, such that all things become the dharma-realm of non-obstruction between phenomena;
this is the Perfect Teaching (the twenty-eighth).
(29) The fourth is the School that Reveals the Doctrine (Xianzong). Following the appearances of light and shadow, it gives rise to attachments to existence and non-existence;

this is called the School of Attachment to Dharmas (Faxiezong). (30) The fifth is the School of Dharma Characteristics (Faxiangzong). It holds that mirror-images, lamp-light, and Buddha-images each exist in their entirety and distinctness. The Buddhas mutually manifest golden images of one another.
Each and every one lacks self-nature; this is called the School of Signlessness (31).

This very lamp-light is empty yet ever-present; this is called the School of Dependent Origination (32). That mirror-reflection is existent yet ever-empty; this is called the School of Quiescent Extinction (33).
The light of five lamps intermingles without being confused; the images of five Buddhas are identical without being separate. The mirror manifests both the Buddhas and the lamps.
Pervading all and containing the inexhaustible is called the School of Perfect Interfusion (34).

Fifth is the Contemplation of the Five Sciences. First, regarding the substance and phenomena upon which one relies: the mirror of the Buddha and the light of a lamp shine through the darkness of subterranean holes, like the dharma-realm of anger in the hells (35).
The mud and darkness within the earth are like the dharma-realm of greed in the hungry ghosts (36).
The darkness of the floor tiles is like the dharma-realm of the delusion of animals. (37) The jars and basins on the ground are like the dharma-realm of the pride of asuras.

(38) The tables and mats within the room are like the dharma-realm of the precepts and virtues of humans. (39) The doors and screens within the room are like the dharma-realm of the meditative concentration of devas.
(40) The darkness of the pillars within the room is like the dharma-realm of the truths of śrāvakas. (41)
The elements (dhātu). (41) The dark rafters upon the roof are like the Pratyekabuddhas’ realization of the dharma-dhātu.
(42) The rafters and planks upon the roof are like the Bodhisattvas’ traversing of the dharma-dhātu. (43) The tiles and windows on the roof are like the Buddhas’ awakening to the dharma-dhātu. (44)
The mirror, lamp, light, and shadow are the teaching; existence and non-existence, as well as their transcendence, are the meaning. This is the correspondence between teaching and meaning.

(45) Appearance is fundamentally illusory and false, termed "phenomenon" (*shi*); nature is fundamentally real and true, termed "principle" (*li*). This is the correspondence between phenomenon and principle. (46) That which is encountered throughout the course of conditions...

The object is called the "field" (viṣaya); that which initiates the contemplation is called "wisdom" (jñāna). This is the correspondence between field and wisdom. (47) Moment-to-moment arising and ceasing is called "activity" (saṃskāra);

that which is not the same in the prior, middle, or subsequent [moments] is called "position" (avasthā). This is the correspondence between activity and position. (48) Initial application and illumination serve as the cause;

the subsequent manifestation of light and shadow serves as the fruit. This is the correspondence between cause and fruit. (49) Abiding securely is the support (āśraya); the mirror-Buddha is the primary (samyak). This is the correspondence between support and primary.

50. "Opposition" (*pratipakṣa*). Fire, copper, and gold take "substance" (*tattva*) as their essence; burning and illuminating forms take "function" (*vṛtti*) as their activity. Essence and function are in opposition. 51.

That which can manifest—such as a mirror or a lamp—is the "person" (*pudgala*); that which is manifested—the reflected image or shadow—is the "phenomenon" (*dharma*). Person and phenomenon are in opposition. 52. Clarity, brightness, and beauty are "conformity" (*ānulomika*);

darkness, concealment, and ugliness are "contrariety" (*pratiloma*). Contrariety and conformity are in opposition. 53. When objective conditions (*viṣaya*) come to meet [the subject], this constitutes...
"Response" (*gan*) refers to the manifestation of images in accordance [with conditions]; it is "correspondence" (*ying*), meaning a responsive correspondence (54).
Next is the contemplation of the dharma upon which one relies: that light and shadows are fundamentally empty is called the "contemplation of true emptiness transcending marks."
The nature of the reflected image is not a void of annihilation; this is called the gate of form as non-annihilated emptiness.

(55) The characteristics of the reflected image are not true emptiness; this is called the gate of form as non-true emptiness. (56) The annihilation-emptiness of the reflected image is in all cases not true emptiness;

this is called the gate of form as emptiness that is not empty. (57) The annihilation-emptiness of the reflected image is in all cases precisely true emptiness; this is called form itself as [true emptiness]. (58)
The Gate of Emptiness (58): These four preceding gates all converge upon the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and return to the true emptiness of the principle-nature (*dharmatā*).

Collectively, they are named "Converging Form to Return to Emptiness"; this is the first section. The gate where severed emptiness is not the nature of images is named "Emptiness is Not Illusory Form" (59).
The gate where true emptiness is not the aspect of images is named "Emptiness is Not Substantial Form" (60). True Emptiness...
That which is not a mere emptiness of severed void, but is the shadow-image [of reality], is called "the gate of emptiness that is not non-form" (61).

That true emptiness which is precisely the shadow-image of severed void is called "the gate of emptiness being form" (62). These four gates above all clarify the rational nature of true emptiness, which is the division of the shadow and light images;
collectively, they are named "clarifying that emptiness is form. This is the second phrase. [The term] "light-image" refers to...

The characteristics [of form]—the entire body—is not different from true emptiness (śūnyatā) which lacks intrinsic nature; true emptiness which lacks intrinsic nature—the entire body—is not different from the characteristics of light and reflected images.
This is called the Gate of the Non-obstruction of Emptiness and Form; it is the third phrase.

(63) This nature of true emptiness is such that form and emptiness are neither identical nor separate, being utterly transcendent and traceless. This is called the Gate of Total Extinction and Non-reliance; it is the fourth phrase. (64)

The characteristics of those reflected images and lights are fused with the substance of fire, copper, and gold, merging without obstruction. This is called the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai guan*).

Gold encompasses the Buddha, the mirror contains the reflection in its entirety, and the lamp penetrates the light; this is termed the gate of "principle pervading phenomena" (*li bian yu shi men*). (65) The Buddha encompasses...

66. Gold, the reflection in a mirror, and the light from a lamp are called the "gate of phenomena pervading principle. 67. Relying upon gold, mirrors, and lamps, the Buddha’s reflections and lights are manifested;
this is called the "gate of principle establishing phenomena. 68. By means of the Buddha’s reflections and lights, the gold, mirrors, and lamps are revealed;
this is called the "gate of phenomena manifesting principle. When one observes the gold and mirrors, no images can be apprehended; this is called...
69. The Gate of Substituting Principle for Phenomena. 70. When seeing shadows and reflections, there is neither lamp nor mirror;
this is called the Gate of Phenomena Being Able to Conceal Principle. 71. In reality, the golden mirror is itself the image; this is called the Gate of True Principle Being Identical to Phenomena.

72. Furthermore, the image-light is itself the golden lamp; this is called the Gate of Phenomenal Dharmas Being Identical to Principle. The substance of the golden mirror and the lamp is not the shadows and lights.
The characteristic [of appearance] is called the gate of ultimate truth and not of phenomena (73). The preceding characteristic of the reflected image is not the substance of the lamp or mirror;
this is called the gate of phenomena and not of principle (74).
Since the fire, copper, and gold can accommodate everything, the light and its reflected images likewise accommodate everything; this is called the "Contemplation of Universal Interpenetration.

Just as the fire, copper, and gold manifest distinctions of size, number, and appearance—such as light and reflected images—this is termed the "Dharma-Gate of Principle Corresponding to Phenomena" (75).
Light and reflected images, like the fire, copper, and gold, are universally pervasive, vast, and penetrate the three periods of time; this is termed...
The gate of phenomena being like true reality (76). A single lamp-light and a single mirror-reflection can extensively contain immeasurable lamp-lights and immeasurable mirror-reflections;

this is called the gate of phenomena containing principle and phenomena (77). Mirror-reflections and lamp-lights do not leave their single location, yet they pervade the ten directions in their entirety;
this is called the gate of the non-obstruction between the universal and the particular (78). The images in the mirror and the lamps do not undergo destruction...
(79) When a single narrow form can contain vast light and shadow, it is called the Gate of Unimpeded Broadness and Narrowness.

(80) When one light and one shadow pervade many other lights and shadows, yet are still able to contain those many other lights and many other shadows, it is called the Gate of Unimpeded Universal Containment.
When those many other lights and shadows are subsumed within this single light and shadow, they immediately enter back into this one.

One light and one shadow are called the Gate of Unimpeded Inclusion (81). One light and one shadow, together with many lights and many shadows, not only can enter into many or one light and shadow, but can also encompass many or one light and shadow;
this is called the Gate of Unimpeded Interpenetration (82). Many lights and many shadows, together with one light and one shadow, not only are that which is encompassed by one...
Many light-shadows. Furthermore, the mutual entry of one and many light-shadows is called the Gate of Non-obstruction of Mutual Presence (83).

The identity of one light-shadow and many light-shadows, wherein the subject that enters and the object that is entered are both fused, is called the Gate of Universal Fusion and Non-obstruction (84).
The simultaneous and sudden manifestation of both the one and the many within a single light-shadow is called the Gate of Simultaneous Fulfillment and Correspondence (85).
To universally contain boundless light-shadows without impairing its own original singular state is called the Gate of Unimpeded Sovereignty over the Broad and the Narrow.

(86) To encompass many shadows within a single shadow, and to encompass a single shadow within many shadows, is called the Gate of the Non-identity of the Mutual Interpenetration of the One and the Many.
(87) When this shadow accommodates that shadow, that is immediately identical to this.
This light-and-shadow pervades that light-and-shadow; this is precisely that. This is called the Gate of the Mutual Identity and Sovereignty of All Dharmas.

(88) When one sees the light-and-shadow of a lamp in an eastern mirror, the east is manifest and the west is hidden. When one sees the light-and-shadow of a lamp in a western mirror, the west is manifest and the east is hidden.
The same principle applies to other directions. This is called the Gate of the Simultaneous Accomplishment of Secrecy, Concealment, and Manifestation. (89) A single mirror’s reflection.
Within [the central mirror], many images of Buddha-light and shadows are accommodated; this is called the "Gate of Subtle Mutual Containment and Establishment" (90).

The light and shadows of the remaining eight mirrors are gathered by the eastern mirror and brought into the western mirror. The western mirror manifests the light and shadows of all the mirrors. This is the case for the eastern and western mirrors, and the same applies to the other mirrors by analogy.
Since the reflections in the mirrors are thus, the repeated manifestation of the lamp-light and Buddha-images is likewise so; this is called the "Cause."
91. The Gate of the Realm of Indra’s Net. Seeing the reflection of a single mirror is itself seeing infinite mirror-reflections;

seeing the light of a single Buddha is itself seeing the light of infinite Buddhas. This is called the Gate of Manifesting the Dharma through Phenomena to Generate Understanding (Tosho-kenhō-shōge-mon).
92. It manifests thus in a single thought-moment. As it is with days and months, so it is with years; as it is with years, so it is with kalpas. The same applies to ages.
The manifestation of months and eons is identical to a single present thought; this is called the "Gate of the Ten Ages as Distinctly Accomplished through the Separation of Dharmas" (93).
A single mirror, a single lamp, and a single Buddha serve as the principal, while the many other mirrors, lamps, and Buddha-images serve as their companions;
this is called the "Gate of the Perfectly Radiant Endowment of Virtue through Principal and Companions" (94).

The mirror, reflection, lamp, and Buddha image constitute the general characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa). (95) Their mutual inclusion as one and many constitutes the specific characteristic (sva-lakṣaṇa).
(96) Sharing a single dependent origination constitutes the common characteristic (tulya-lakṣaṇa). (97) Their mutual non-confusion constitutes the distinct characteristic (bheda-lakṣaṇa).

(98) The convergence of the one and many to first produce the mirror-reflection constitutes the productive characteristic (utpatti-lakṣaṇa). (99) The mirror, lamp, and Buddha image each return to their own source.
Position is a characteristic of disintegration (100).
If one can carefully and thoroughly examine these hundred gateways of Dharma and analogies, then the other ten-by-ten inexhaustible Dharma-gateways [will become clear].
There is nothing that is not suddenly and completely penetrated.
